bio.en: Evan Spiegel is the co-founder and CEO of Snap, the company behind Snapchat—one of the very few durable consumer social apps ever built, with over one billion monthly active users and more than $6 billion in annual revenue.
bio.zh: Evan Spiegel 是 Snap 的联合创始人兼 CEO；Snap 是 Snapchat 的母公司——Snapchat 是有史以来极少数真正长期存活的消费者社交应用之一，月活用户超 10 亿，年收入超 60 亿美元。

summary.en: Evan argues the hardest part of consumer products isn't product-market fit but distribution, and that Snap's relentless innovation (Stories, AR glasses, swipe navigation) comes from a deliberately tiny design team that presents work on day one. He reflects on 15 years of being copied by the industry and why 'software is not a moat'—a lesson the AI world is now rediscovering. Framing the year as a 'crucible moment,' he stresses that humanity, not technology, dictates adoption, and warns of major societal pushback against careless AI deployment.
summary.zh: Evan 认为消费品最难的部分不是产品市场契合，而是分发；Snap 持续不断的创新（Stories、AR 眼镜、滑动导航）来自一支刻意保持精简、入职第一天就要展示作品的设计团队。他回顾了 15 年来被全行业抄袭的经历，以及为何“软件不是护城河”——这正是如今 AI 界正在重新学到的教训。他把这一年称为“熔炉时刻”，强调决定技术能否被采用的终究是人，而非技术本身，并警示对草率部署 AI 将会出现巨大的社会反弹。

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Well, I think it's really interesting in terms of the examples that you just shared of TikTok and threads, because you just shared two examples of people who figured out distribution. And I think that that's actually one of the hardest things to figure out in consumer technology today. We were so fortunate when we created Snapchat, the mobile phone and the app store were just getting started. So people were downloading lots of new apps all the time. They were really excited about trying new services. Instagram, I think it started a year before Snapchat or something like that. So there was a real appetite to try new apps and new services. And that's not the case today. It's a lot harder to get distribution for new ideas and new services. People aren't downloading as many apps now as they used to. And both TikTok and Threads figured out distribution, which is why I think there are more recent examples of success. (00:04:09): TikTok did it with money, which I actually thought was really innovative. They spent billions of dollars subsidizing both sides of their video marketplace, acquiring customers to watch videos and then paying creators to make videos. And so they were able to bootstrap their ecosystem. And I think with Threads, obviously, they were able to leverage the amazing distribution that Meta has across all of their other products. So I think so much of consumer technology focuses on, am I building the right product? Do I have product market fit? (00:04:51): So as I reflect on the early days of building Snapchat, the thing that we figured out in terms of distribution, especially when it comes to social, was that back then people believed that there were network effects and social networks that meant that the more people you had using the service, the stickier that it is. (00:05:11): And so there was no way to beat the biggest networks because those were the most valuable. And what Snapchat figured out that was, I think, different was that despite the fact that there were much bigger networks that connected more people, what really mattered was connecting you to the right people. And so if you could just connect someone, not to all their friends, but to their best friend, to their partner, to their spouse, the people that they cared most about in the world, that's where the majority of the value is in the network. And so that's what really allowed us to grow in those early days. We had the benefit of the app store and mobile distribution, but we also had a different way of growing our service, which wasn't about having the most friends. It was about having your close friends.

turns.en: It's certainly better than making stuff that people don't want to copy. (00:11:18): And then it also informed a lot of our thinking about investing in other places that are really hard to copy, including hardware, where it's really, really challenging to copy our fully vertically integrated stack around augmented reality. So I'm certain there's a lot more to talk about there, but I think we learned early on that software's easy to copy, and so it's really important to build more durable modes.
turns.zh: 相比之下，开发人们不想模仿的产品当然更糟糕。所以我认为，从很多方面来说，我们能够持续创新，创造出真正能引起用户共鸣、最终让人们愿意模仿Snap的产品，这确实是一种幸运。但这也意味着我们必须要深思熟虑我们的战略。过去15年对我来说是一个很有趣的反思期，因为15年前，我们发现软件本身并非护城河——而这正是当今所有人都在AI领域逐渐意识到的问题。但15年前，我们的软件功能很容易被竞争对手克隆，因此我们开始思考如何建立更持久的业务，如何构建更大、更高效的商业模式。（00:10:44）：我们最先做的一件事就是大力构建生态系统，无论是创作者与Snap用户之间的关系，还是围绕增强现实打造的平台（开发者在此平台上开发了数百万个镜头）。软件功能很容易被复制，但完整的生态系统或平台却很难被模仿或复制。因此我们意识到，越是能围绕我们的业务构建平台，越是能与创作者和开发者共同构建生态系统，别人就越难简单地模仿我们。（00:11:18）：这也影响了我们对其他难以复制领域的投资决策，比如硬件领域。要想复制我们的全垂直整合的增强现实硬件堆栈，难度极大。我相信这里还有很多值得探讨的地方，但我们很早就意识到软件容易被复制，因此构建更持久的商业模式至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's really interesting hearing this from you. And I was going to get to this later, but we can talk about this now, this big investment you've been putting into hardware. You would think network effects would be the moat. That's what everybody's always trying to get to because that's classically a great moat. Are you saying that that's maybe not even as great a moat or that's just not enough and then you need something more like say hardware?
turns.zh: 听你这么说真是很有意思。我本来想等会儿再谈这个，但现在我们可以聊聊你们在硬件领域的大规模投资。人们可能会认为网络效应才是护城河。这是大家一直追求的目标，因为传统上这就是一个很棒的护城河。你是说这甚至可能不是那么好的护城河，或者说这还不够，所以还需要硬件之类的？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: I think network effects are certainly an important piece of the puzzle for sure, but I don't think they're enough when it comes to these sorts of software cloning. And so despite the fact that we've got a ton of patents and we protected all these ideas, the way that it works in software is that it's quite easy for folks to copy or iterate on top of these ideas. And so I think in addition to network effects, it's really important to try to build businesses that are more defensible by truly building out a platform that can support relationships between creators, developers, and the community, because that in and of itself we found is incredibly difficult to copy.
turns.zh: 我认为网络效应当然是拼图中重要的一块，但对于这类软件克隆来说，它还不够。因此，尽管我们拥有大量专利，也保护了所有这些创意，但软件行业的运作方式是，人们很容易复制或改进这些创意。所以我认为，除了网络效应，真正建立一个更具防御性的业务，真正构建一个能支持创作者、开发者和社区之间关系的平台，这非常重要，因为我们发现这本身就很难被复制。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so interesting. If you think about it, you're working on two of the hardest types of businesses, a consumer social platform and hardware. And I love that you're doing that. And this hardware investment, you've been at it for a long time. You had spectacles, you had drones. I don't think people are remembering yet this drone that could take photos of you. And then you have specs coming out. Is it specs or spectacles the name of what's coming out today, by the way?
turns.zh: 真是太有趣了。仔细想想，你正在经营两项最具挑战性的业务——消费者社交平台和硬件产品。我很欣赏你能坚持做这两件事。说到硬件投资，你已经深耕这个领域很久了。你曾推出过眼镜产品，还有无人机。人们可能还不太记得那款能给你拍照的无人机。现在又要推出眼镜了，顺便问一下，你们今天推出的产品叫什么名字？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Specs is coming out this year.
turns.zh: 今年要推出Specs产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Specs.
turns.zh: Specs。

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. We're going to talk about it, but just maybe you've already answered it, why this is something you're so passionate about, but why this kind of ongoing investment in hardware?
turns.zh: 好的，不错。我们接下来要聊聊这个话题，但或许你已经回答过了，为什么你对硬件领域如此热情？为什么要持续投资硬件产品？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Well, I think to take a huge step back, I love computers. I grew up using computers all the time. I built my own computer when I was in middle school. I fell in love with graphic design and would spend every lunch period in the computer lab. And I think one of the things that I noticed about computers and I think today with mobile phones is that in many ways they isolate us from one another. They actually take us out of our social interactions. They took me off the playground at recess and put me into the computer lab. Or if I look at our 15-year-old today and his friends, sometimes when they're hanging out, they're all looking down at their phones, even though they're all together. And so I think there's just such a big opportunity to build technology that actually brings us together, that keeps us grounded in the real world rather than removing us from it. (00:14:03): And that's something that we realized early on with Snapchat. We were innovating, building lenses and augmented reality, but ultimately we saw that people were using AR on these tiny little phone screens that required you to use your thumbs to interact. And so it was almost like interacting with the world through a keyhole rather than actually staying grounded and being able to interact together with friends. So it just seems so obvious that as computers play a bigger and bigger role in our lives, I think today people spend seven or eight hours a day on average on screens that something has got to change to make this technology fit better into our lives. We get enormous value from computers, but at the same time, I think the cost is quite meaningful and I think they need to evolve. So with the early version of Spectacles, I guess that was back in 2014 or something like that, the initial idea was just to get the camera off the phone out of your pocket and allow you to more easily take snaps out in the world. (00:15:04): But we've then sort of built a roadmap from there where we added a second camera to get depth. We added a display to be able to overlay digital objects into the world and help you interact with them. And then with the last generation in 2024, we released our operating system, which now allows developers to build full featured software inside of specs in preparation for the consumer launch. So I don't know, I think the time is right for a new type of computer. I think people are frustrated with the cost of using phones and computers today. They're kind of all hunched over like gremlins and we can build a new computer. (00:15:42): We have built a new computer that brings people outside, that helps them connect together with their friends, that frees them up to actually use their hands to interact with the world. And that to me is really exciting. I think it's a whole new chapter. And gosh, I mean, what? It's been 20 years or something since the iPhone. So it's about time for something new, I think.
turns.zh:
嗯，我觉得先退一步说，我热爱电脑。我从小就一直用电脑。中学时我自己组装过电脑。我深深爱上了平面设计，每天午餐时间都会泡在计算机实验室里。我发现电脑（以及如今的手机）在很多方面把我们彼此隔离开来，让我们的社交互动变得越来越少。比如说我小时候在课间休息时被电脑实验室吸引走，无法参与操场上的活动；而如今的15岁青少年和他们的朋友们聚会时，尽管大家身处同一空间，却都低头玩手机。这让我意识到，科技应该能真正把人们聚集在一起，让我们扎根于现实世界，而不是被割裂开来。

（00:14:03）这也是我们早期开发Snapchat时意识到的问题。我们不断创新，开发镜头和增强现实功能，但最终发现用户在小小的手机屏幕上使用AR技术，需要用拇指操作，仿佛透过锁孔观察世界，而非真正沉浸于社交互动中。随着计算机在生活中扮演越来越重要的角色，人们平均每天花7到8小时盯着屏幕，显然这种局面必须改变。我们从中获得了巨大价值，但代价也显而易见——技术需要进化。

（00:15:04）早期版本的Spectacles（2014年左右）最初的设想是让相机从手机中解放出来，让人们更方便地拍摄现实场景。但后来我们逐步优化：增加第二个摄像头获取深度信息，添加显示屏将数字对象叠加到现实环境中，帮助用户与之互动。2024年发布的最新一代产品更是推出操作系统，支持开发者在设备内开发全功能应用，为消费级发布做准备。

（00:15:42）我认为现在是时候打造新型的计算设备了。人们对当下手机和电脑的使用成本感到不满，人们像小精灵一样低头玩手机，我们需要创造新的计算方式。我们的新设备能让人们走出家门，与朋友互动，用双手探索世界。这对我来说非常激动人心。这将开启全新的篇章。天啊，自iPhone问世以来已经20年了，是时候迎来新的突破了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I got an early preview of the specs and it's extremely cool. I learned how to be an air bender. I put plants all over my house drawing all over the place and there's multiplayer features, which is very cool, which I think is part of the idea, is you're connecting with people versus sitting in a VR environment on your own. I worry about being connected all the time. So I imagine that's like a new thing we have to figure out. How do we not just get hooked on just watching things onto the side instead of looking at someone with? Do you have any thoughts there? Just is there a solution to that other than just like social norms?
turns.zh: 嗯，我提前看到了一些技术规格参数，真的太棒了。我学会了如何控制空气元素。我在家里到处摆放植物，到处涂鸦，还有多人游戏功能，这太酷了。我觉得这正是设计理念的一部分——你需要与他人互动，而不是独自沉浸在虚拟现实环境中。我担心自己会沉迷于这些功能，所以我想这是一个我们需要解决的新问题。如何避免只顾着看虚拟内容而忽略现实的人呢？你对此有什么看法吗？除了社交规范，还有其他解决办法吗？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: I do think social norms will play a big role, but I also think one of the things people experience with AR, specs, unlike these heads up display glasses, they don't just put an annoying little screen that's stuck to your face on the glasses. They actually anchor content in the world, which is really different. They put that content directly in your field of view rather than requiring you to look down at some little screen or get some text alert or notification. So I think, frankly, I don't think those use cases are very compelling. I don't think receiving phone notifications on your face is a valuable proposition for most folks. So I don't think we necessarily have to worry about that because I think most people don't want that. I think what is going to be really important with specs is showing people all of the incredible new ways they can hang out and connect together with their friends wearing specs, but I don't think it'll be disruptive or notification based or something like that. (00:17:35): One of the things that I really dislike about the heads-up display glasses is when you're looking at the little heads up display in the corner, you're actually looking at your friend's crotch while you're talking to them if you check the heads up display. So the position is just very strange. And I don't think that that's something that really is resonating with customers, nor do I think that's something that's going to become like a widespread behavior.
turns.zh: 我确实认为社交规范会起很大作用，但我也认为AR眼镜与那些头戴式显示器不同。AR眼镜不会在眼镜上加一个烦人的小屏幕，而是将内容直接锚定在现实世界中，这点很不同。它们把内容直接呈现在你的视野里，而不是要求你低头看小屏幕、接收文字提醒或通知。所以说实话，我觉得这些用例不是很吸引人。对大多数人来说，手机通知出现在脸上并不是一个有价值的提议。所以我觉得我们不必为此担忧，因为我认为大多数人并不想要那样。我认为AR眼镜真正重要的是向人们展示佩戴眼镜后与朋友们聚会和互动的各种新奇方式，但我不认为它会颠覆现有模式或基于通知功能之类的。（00:17:35）：我对头戴式显示器最不满的一点是，当你看角落里的小显示屏时，如果你看向对方，就会发现自己正盯着对方的裤裆。所以这个位置设计得非常奇怪。我觉得这既不受用户欢迎，也不太可能成为一种普遍的行为。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to go back to this idea of how to innovate. I feel like Snap has always been punching above its weight in terms of just how much new stuff comes out of your team, how many inventions happen considering the size of the company and the history. What do you find needs to be true for innovation to happen? What do you do to allow for all these great ideas to emerge?
turns.zh: 我想再回到创新这个话题。我觉得Snap在创新方面一直表现出色——考虑到公司的规模和历史，团队能推出这么多新东西，创造出如此多的创新成果，这确实令人惊叹。要让创新发生，你认为需要满足哪些条件？你做了哪些努力来让这些优秀的创意涌现出来？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: The best sort of academic overview or summary I think comes from a guy, Safi Bahcall, who wrote a book called Loon Shots. It's really worth reading. It's all about the innovation process. And actually when I read it, I was like, "Oh my gosh, that kind of explains a lot of how we think about innovation at Snap." And I think to summarize the academic version, we can talk about what we've developed and built at Snap, but to summarize, essentially his findings are that basically if you want to deliver a product at scale, you usually need quite a large organization. A large organization needs hierarchy and structure, a lot of operational rigor. And as soon as you have an organization that's very large and very structured like that, people become very focused on getting a promotion, getting into the next step of the hierarchy. And that means that all of a sudden they become a lot more risk averse. (00:19:13): They're not really as willing to try new things. They're very focused on achieving the goals that have sort of been set for them in this operational hierarchy, and that makes it very, very challenging to innovate. Now on the flip side, structures that are really healthy and constructive for innovation typically are very, very flat. That's the same for our design team, for example, where there's no one that has a fancier title or a role. There's a lot of flexibility in terms of the ability to try new things and fail quickly and put up crazy ideas. And what he basically finds is that the companies that are very successful actually have both types of organizations inside their company and that the leaders of the organization are the ones who are responsible for creating a healthy functioning relationship between the two types of organizations. Because what ends up happening in a lot of companies is that the small innovative team becomes critical of the large organization, oh, they're so bureaucratic and slow, they don't innovate, things like that. (00:20:14): And then the larger organization is like, "Oh, what are these Jokers doing?" Just innovating, they're not really driving the business, they're not supporting our customers. And so a lot of tension actually arises from the different organizational structures. And so the leadership responsibility, and I think Safi does a really good job looking throughout history, what leaders have cultivated really constructive and powerful relationships between the more innovative or flat parts of the organization and the more structured and hierarchical parts of the organization, how you create that mutual respect, how you create that dialogue between those parts of the organization is so important. And so when I read that, I was like, wow, that actually sounds quite similar to what we have at Snap. We have to run a large public company, serve almost a billion customers. That means our service needs to be really reliable and it means that we need to operate really, really effectively to serve our customers. (00:21:08): And at the same time, we have a very, very small ... It sort of oscillates between like nine and 12 people design team that is constantly innovating and creating new things. And I think the beauty of what I love about Snap is that the dialogue between those two teams is where a lot of that innovation happens because a lot of our engineers working to serve our customers or working on reliability have a bunch of great ideas and so do our designers. And as long as they're in dialogue, really great things can happen.
turns.zh:
我认为最棒的学术综述或总结来自萨菲·巴赫卡尔（Safi Bahcall），他写了一本名为《Loon Shots》的书。这本书非常值得一读，核心内容是关于创新过程的。当我读这本书时，内心感叹："天哪，这本书解释了我们在Snap公司对创新的诸多理解！"  

要概括学术版本的核心观点：我们在Snap开发和构建的创新体系，实质上与巴赫卡尔的研究成果高度契合——即若想大规模推出产品，通常需要庞大的组织架构。大规模组织必然需要层级和结构，强调运营的严谨性。但当组织规模过大、过于规范化后，人们会过度关注晋升和进入下一层级，这导致创新意愿骤降。（00:19:13）他们不再愿意尝试新事物，仅专注于完成运营层级设定的目标，创新因此举步维艰。  

反之，真正有益创新的组织架构通常极为扁平化。以我们的设计团队为例，没有任何头衔或角色特权，成员拥有极高的灵活性，能够快速试验疯狂想法。巴赫卡尔发现，最成功的公司内部同时存在两种组织类型，而领导者需要在两者之间建立健康的协作关系。  

（00:20:14）许多公司中，创新团队会对庞大组织抱怨官僚主义、效率低下等问题；而大型组织则质疑创新团队不务正业、不支持业务与客户。组织结构的冲突实则源于领导层的失职。巴赫卡尔通过历史案例，深刻剖析领导者如何在创新与秩序之间建立相互尊重的对话机制。  

读完这些论述，我深有共鸣：Snap既要运营大型上市公司，服务近十亿用户，保障服务可靠性和运营效率；又要维持由9至12人组成的创新团队，持续创造新价值。两者之间的对话机制正是创新源泉所在——客户服务工程师和设计师的创意火花在此碰撞，推动着Snap不断前行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's someone, I forget who this was, but they described this approach as the fast thinking and slow thinking part of the organization, kind of like Kahneman's System 1, System 2 approach. It's interesting, the fast moving, let's say. What do you kind of call this innovation team or do you have a label for this like, let's come up with the new ideas part of the org?
turns.zh: 有人（我忘了是谁）把这种方法描述为组织中的快速思维和慢速思维部分，有点像卡尼曼的系统1和系统2理论。很有意思，比如说快速行动的部分。你们怎么称呼这个创新团队？或者有没有专门的称呼来指代组织中负责提出新想法的部门？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Well, I think it's really important to acknowledge that new ideas come from everywhere and we want that. But I think the design team in particular, it's really important, and we call it the design team, it's really important that they have a flat non-hierarchical structure where new ideas can come from anywhere. I mean, I think that that is absolutely critical.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为必须承认，新想法来自各处，这一点很重要，我们也希望如此。但我觉得设计团队尤其重要，我们称之为设计团队，他们拥有平等无层级的架构，让新想法能从任何地方涌现，这一点至关重要。我认为这绝对是关键所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So in terms of how you operationalize this, is that the key to the innovation you've seen as this specific small design team who can work? Talk about just how you actually operationalize this sort of way of working.
turns.zh: 那么，在实际操作层面，你们是如何实现这种创新的呢？比如说，这个能够高效运作的小型设计团队，关键之处在哪里？能否谈谈如何具体落实这种工作方式？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I think it's an important part of it, but a lot of how we built Snap was modeled actually on mine and Bobby's original relationship, right? Where Bobby has a computer science, heavy duty computer science and stats background, mathematical and computational science, but he really likes design and likes thinking about building things for customers and empathizing with them. I have a design background, right? I was in the product design program back at school, which actually was part of the mechanical engineering department at the time. I took some computer science classes, so I sort of knew what I was talking about when it came to computer science. So we both had mutual respect for each other and our skillsets and our backgrounds and both enjoyed talking together about the types of products we wanted to create. And that dialogue created a lot of innovation. (00:23:16): And so a lot of how we've thought about growing the company over time is like strengthening that dialogue between engineers and designers and creating an environment where folks feel comfortable throwing out really crazy ideas. But I think for the design team in particular, the thing that is probably most important is the velocity of design work. So I typically meet with our designers for a couple hours every week and we just look at work. I mean, new work every week, hundreds of ideas, I would guess, on a weekly basis that to me, if I think about where I learned how to design and build things, I have sort of an interesting combination because I went to Stanford for the product design program, which is really focused on empathy and this iterative process of understanding what people want and building prototypes and iterating, but really centered on empathy, human centered design. (00:24:09): And then at the same time, I'd also been to art school. So I had studied at art center, I'd studied at Otis here in Los Angeles, both great art schools. And so I was used to this grinding expectation that you're making new work all the time and then just an absolutely brutal critique process on a regular basis. And so for me, as I thought about the parts of my education that I really liked, it was this combination of really developing empathy with people and the types of products that they want in their lives, but at the same time, having this really high velocity work ethic where you're not just like thinking all the time about new products, you're actually making stuff every week, all the time, and then you're talking about it as a team because that critique process is where so much of the learning sort of happens. (00:24:58): So I would say that the velocity of work is really important because our favorite saying is, if you want to have a good idea, you have to have lots of ideas. That's really, really important.
turns.zh:
是啊。我觉得这很重要，但我们开发Snap的很多思路实际上是基于我和鲍比最初的合作关系，对吧？鲍比拥有计算机科学、重型计算和统计学背景，精通数学和计算科学，但他特别喜欢设计，喜欢为客户构思产品并设身处地为用户着想。我则有设计背景——我曾就读于斯坦福大学的产品设计项目，当时这个项目隶属于机械工程系。我也上过一些计算机科学课程，所以在计算机科学领域还是略知一二的。我们对彼此的技能和背景都心怀敬意，喜欢一起探讨想打造的产品类型。这种对话催生了诸多创新。（00:23:16）  
所以，我们一直致力于如何推动公司发展，其中很重要的一点就是加强工程师与设计师之间的对话，并营造一个让大家能畅所欲言、提出疯狂想法的环境。但对设计团队而言，最关键的或许是设计工作的效率。我每周都会和设计师们开几个小时的会，一起审视新作品。每周都有数百个创意想法，这让我想起自己是如何学会设计和产品开发的。我有着独特的教育背景——我曾就读于斯坦福大学的产品设计项目，这个项目强调共情、迭代式理解用户需求并制作原型，但核心是以人为本的设计。（00:24:09）  
与此同时，我还上过艺术学校，比如洛杉矶的奥蒂斯艺术设计学院。这些顶尖艺术学府培养了高强度创作习惯：每周都要产出新作品，并接受严格的点评。这让我意识到，教育中最宝贵的部分在于培养对用户需求的共情能力，同时保持高效的工作节奏——每周不断迭代产品，并在团队中进行讨论，因为点评环节正是学习的关键环节。（00:24:58）  
我认为工作效率至关重要。我们常说：要想产生好点子，就必须先产生大量想法。这点非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I just had Keith Rabois on the podcast. I don't know if you know this about his ... He has many contrarian takes. One is if you're building a consumer product, do not talk to customers. Not only is it not useful, his advice is, its harmful because it can infiltrate your subconscious and it just doesn't lead to great things. What's your perspective on that?
turns.zh: 我最近在播客上邀请了基思·拉博伊斯。他有很多逆向观点，其中一个是关于开发消费产品时不要和用户交流。他认为这不仅没用，还会潜移默化地影响你的思维，阻碍创新。你怎么看？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Wow, that's really interesting. I would say you have to talk to customers, you have to share your idea, you should share your idea as quickly as possible, as frequently as possible. It doesn't mean you need to take people's advice or feedback, but it's really important, I think, to listen. And I think for me, it's not like the survey model of listening. I don't think that's particularly helpful. But I think going deep and talking with someone for an hour, two hours about how do they use technology, how does it fit in their lives? How do they feel about the products they're using? You can learn so much. And I think customers are an endless source of inspiration when it comes to building products.
turns.zh: 哇，这真的很有趣。我觉得你必须和客户交流，分享你的想法，而且要尽可能快、尽可能频繁地分享。但这并不意味着你需要采纳别人的建议或反馈，但我认为倾听对方的意见非常重要。对我而言，这不是那种传统的调查式倾听模式——我觉得那没多大用处。但深入交流、与某人畅谈一两个小时——比如他们如何使用科技产品，科技产品如何融入他们的生活？他们对正在使用的产品有何感受？你能收获很多见解。在产品开发方面，客户永远是灵感的源泉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So pro talking to users, because I feel like you've been really good at just like, here's what it'll be and here's how it should be. And even though people may not understand this is what it should be, I trust me it'll work really well. What's that balance of just like, here's what I'll pay attention to, here's what I won't.
turns.zh: 所以，专业地与用户交流很重要，因为我觉得你过去一直是那种“这就是它应该有的样子，这就是它应该有的功能”的模式。即便人们可能不理解这才是正确的方案，我相信它最终会大获成功。如何平衡这种“我会关注这些方面，我不会关注那些方面”的思路呢？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Well, let's use stories as an example, right? So back then, we were hearing from customers all the time, "I want to send all button. I want to send an all button." It's so annoying to select everybody on my list of friends and Snapchat. If you just give me a send all button, then I can blast snaps to everybody all day long and that'd be really great. And at the same time, we were talking to people about their use of social media and they're like, "Oh gosh, social media, I feel all this pressure. Everything I put up there is permanent all the time. It's got all these likes and comments, so there's all this judgment. So I only feel like I can put pretty and perfect things up there and I just don't like that pressure. That doesn't feel good." I actually love the way that Snapchat allows me to just express myself and share with my friends without that sort of judgment and pressure. (00:27:07): And so, we thought that was really interesting. And so we dug deeper into how people were using social media. We found that one of the things they thought was really weird was that everything was in reverse chronological order in the feed. So the feed, back in the day, the timeline, right? When people posted photos, they would always find that the end of the birthday party appeared first in the feed and then the middle and then the beginning of the party. So everything was sort of just played in reverse in the feed, which was really strange to folks. So we listened to all of that and heard all of that, but then we came up with something totally new and different, which were stories that were responsive to the feedback. They didn't create a send to all button, but they did create a way to easily share with all of your friends without spamming them all day long. (00:27:52): They removed public metrics. They didn't have likes and comments and things like that to reduce pressure. They disappeared after 24 hours so that everyone could start the day fresh again the next day. And they, maybe most importantly, were in chronological order, which is the way that people have told stories since the beginning of time. So I think that's an example where listening is incredibly valuable. All of those insights that we received just from listening to folks made a huge difference in the product design process, but we didn't build exactly what they asked for. We empathized and then came up with something new.
turns.zh: 好吧，以故事为例。当时我们不断收到用户反馈：“我想要一个群发按钮。我想要一个群发按钮。”在Snapchat上选择所有好友列表实在太烦人了。如果你能给我一个群发按钮，我就能一整天把快拍狂发给所有人，那简直太棒了。与此同时，我们和用户讨论他们的社交媒体使用习惯时，他们会说：“天哪，社交媒体让我压力山大。每发布一条内容都要永久保留，还有那些点赞和评论，处处是评判。所以我只能把完美无缺的东西放上去，但这种压力真让人受不了。” 而我却特别喜欢Snapchat能让我自由表达、与朋友分享，而无需承受这种压力和评判。（00:27:07）于是我们深入探究用户的社交媒体使用习惯，发现他们觉得最奇怪的一点是信息流中的倒序排列。过去的信息流，时间线对吧，当人们发布照片时，生日派对的结尾总是出现在信息流的首页，然后是中间部分，再到开头部分。整个信息流就像倒放一样，这对用户来说很不习惯。于是我们倾听了这些反馈，提出了全新的解决方案——故事功能。故事功能响应了用户需求，没有添加群发按钮，却提供了轻松与所有朋友分享的途径，而无需整天狂发消息。（00:27:52）他们移除了公开数据，不再显示点赞和评论等数据以减少压力，故事24小时后自动消失，让用户第二天能重新开始。最重要的是，故事采用了按时间顺序排列的模式，这是人类讲述故事的天然方式。所以我认为这就是倾听的价值所在。我们从倾听用户中获得的这些洞见为产品设计过程带来了巨大改变，但我们并没有完全按照他们的要求去建造产品。我们先感同身受，再创新。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that's such a great story. I love hearing these stories of features that everyone's using now and how they came to be. Was there a moment of just like, this is the way, the story concept that you remember or was it kind of this very gradual evolution?
turns.zh: 太棒了！我特别喜欢听这些故事——听人们讲述如今大家都在用的功能背后的诞生历程。是某个瞬间灵光一现，还是一个渐进的演变过程呢？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: It was iterative because in a lot of ways, some of the early ideas started more around a status update that was sort of like, how could you know what your friends on Snapchat were up to even if you weren't sending Snaps back and forth? And so it sort of started there. And then again, through talking to people and iterating, understanding what folks were really looking for, we ended up with stories and some of the gestures that people maybe take for granted today, being able to tap forward through stories and backwards through stories, full screen, vertical content. Those were all really new things at the time.
turns.zh: 这个过程是迭代式的。最初的想法源于如何让用户即便不互发快拍，也能了解好友在Snapchat上的动态。于是我们从这个点出发。通过不断与用户交流、迭代产品，逐渐形成了如今的快拍功能和一些被视为理所当然的交互设计，比如前后滑动切换快拍、全屏体验、竖屏内容等。在当时这些都是创新性的设计。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there another story of something that y'all built that just was interesting and of how it came to be? These stories are so interesting and people don't know these histories.
turns.zh: 有没有其他你们团队开发的有趣功能，以及它们背后的故事？这些故事太吸引人了，而人们往往不了解背后的故事。

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: One of my favorite stories was around screenshot detection actually in the early days because when we first built Snapchat and we shared with people, "Oh, you could send photos that disappear." Everyone said, "No, you can't. You can always take a screenshot. What do you mean you can send things that disappear? That makes no sense." And so we thought a lot, I remember that summer after school, we went home, we were working out at my dad's house and Bobby and I were just going back and forth and we were like ... We were having fun using the product. We were sending photos back and forth, but people would just keep saying, "Well, it's not about disappearing photos because you can just save them. I don't get it." (00:29:55): And one of the things we invented that at the time, we figured out a way, we realized that if you were pressing and holding to open a snap and left your finger on the screen and you took a screenshot, it would basically trigger an event on the phone essentially that made ... The phone would essentially report that your finger had lost contact with the screen.That's what the screenshot mechanism did. (00:30:20): So even though Apple didn't provide an API at the time to let you know that a screenshot had been taken, there was a way for us to essentially detect this touch event to learn that a screenshot had happened. And then we would just send a notification back to the sender that, oh, the recipient had taken a screenshot. And that for us in the early days really resonated with our community because they didn't mind if somebody saved one of their Snaps, they just wanted to know. And I think that that early invention was one of the first things that really got a lot of traction in the early days and I think helped Snapchat spread as a new way of communicating.
turns.zh: 我最喜欢的故事之一是早期关于截图检测的研发。刚推出Snapchat时，我们向别人演示功能时大家都说：“照片发出去就消失了？不行啊，你随时都能截图。”我们苦思冥想，记得那个暑假结束后，我和Bobby在老爸家健身时反复测试，边玩边讨论。用户总说：“照片消失？你随时能保存啊，我不明白。”（00:29:55）后来我们发现，用户长按打开快拍时，如果手指离开屏幕再截图，手机会触发事件报告手指脱离屏幕，这就是截图机制的原理。（00:30:20）虽然苹果当时没有提供API检测截图，但我们通过触摸事件识别截图行为，并向发送者反馈对方截图了照片。这项功能在早期引发了用户共鸣——他们不介意别人保存快拍，只想知道对方是否截图。这项创新是早期吸引用户的重要突破，也助力Snapchat成为新型社交方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that is really cool. I can't imagine Snapchat existing without you figuring that out. That feels like such a core mechanic. Something that is also really, I'd say famous in the PM community about Snap is you guys waited a long time to hire product managers. I've done all these research reports on just like how long it took the top companies to hire their PMs. And the number I saw is you had 200 employees before you hired your first PM. I'm curious if you think that was a mistake waiting that long and just your current thoughts on product managers, just like how they fit into Snap. A lot of people listening to this are PMs and so I'm just curious how you feel.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我无法想象如果不是你发现了这个点子，Snapchat还能存在下去。这感觉就像是核心机制一样。说到这，我想在产品经理（PM）社区里，关于Snap的一个广为人知的故事是，你们等了很久才聘请产品经理。我做过很多研究报告，调查顶尖公司聘请PM的时机。数据显示，你们在聘请首位PM之前，公司已经有200名员工了。我很好奇，你是否认为等待太久是个错误？或者你对产品经理的看法如何？他们在Snap的定位又是什么？很多听众都是PM，所以我很想听听你的见解。

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: A lot of my view of product management was actually driven by my view of designers and the role that designers should play. And one of the things that I was concerned about in the tech community, if you look at the traditional tech org structure, designers really are producing visuals. They're not really producing the product direction or the strategy or the vision or net new innovation. They're really responsive actually, I think in many cases to the PM saying, "This is what we're building. Now go make me some visuals." And I absolutely did not want that type of culture to take root because again, as I mentioned, we modeled a lot of the way that we develop products here at Snap on that early relationship between myself and Bobby, really this harmonious relationship between design and engineering and how important that is, that dialogue is to building great things and great products. (00:32:28): And so I think in the early days, my view was not that we don't need PMs, my view is that designers should do that work. So that's essentially what we would say to our designers, which was like, "Hey, if you need PM support, why don't you just do it yourself? What's the big deal?" And I think that that really helped, frankly, designers play a more active role in the product development process. (00:32:49): Now, today at a company operating at our scale, if you look at the legal requirements, our approach to trust and safety, it really does take a village to get a new product off the ground and product managers play a really important coordination role in all that in addition to synthesizing, for example, data science analysis and bringing together the working group to try to solve problems or innovate or make the product better. So I think as the organization grows and there becomes all of these different capabilities that the company didn't have in the early days, whether it's data science, you name it, product managers play a really important role in bringing all those folks to the table and making sure we deliver the right thing at the right time.
turns.zh:
我对产品管理的很多看法实际上源于我对设计师及其角色的理解。在科技社区里，我一直担忧传统的组织结构中，设计师只是负责视觉设计。他们并未真正参与产品方向、战略规划或创新构思。相反，他们更多是在响应PM的需求，比如“我们要开发这个产品，现在快去给我设计界面”。我坚决反对这种文化模式，因为正如我提到的，Snap早期产品开发模式建立在鲍比和我之间的深厚合作之上——设计与工程之间的和谐协作对打造卓越产品至关重要。（00:32:28）  
在初期阶段，我认为问题不在于不需要PM，而是设计师应该承担这些工作。我们对设计师的要求是：“如果需要PM支持，为何不自己完成？有什么大不了的？”这种理念确实帮助设计师在产品开发过程中发挥了更积极的作用。（00:32:49）  
如今，在规模如此之大的公司里，面对法律合规要求和安全信任体系，开发新产品确实需要多方协作。PM在此过程中起着关键的协调作用，比如整合数据科学分析结果，召集团队共同解决问题、创新改进产品。随着公司发展壮大，涌现出许多早期缺乏的能力——无论是数据科学还是其他领域，PM在整合各方资源、确保按时交付正确成果方面都发挥着重要作用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I am so excited to tell you about this season's supporting sponsor Vanta. Vanta helps over 15,000 companies like Cursor, Ramp, Duolingo, Snowflake, and Atlassian earn and prove trust with their customers. Teams are building and shipping products faster than ever thanks to AI. But as a result, the amount of risk being introduced into your product and your business is higher than it's ever been. Every security leader that I talk to is feeling the increasing weight of protecting their organization, their business, and not to mention their customer data. Because things are moving so fast, they are constantly reacting, having to guess at priorities, and having to make do with outdated solutions. (00:34:14): Vanta automates compliance and risk management with over 35 security and privacy frameworks, including SOC two, ISO 27001, and HIPAA. This helps companies get compliant, fast, and stay compliant. More than ever before, trust has the power to make or break your business. Learn more at vanta.com/lenny. And as a listener of this podcast, you get $1,000 off Vanta. That's vanta.com/lenny. (00:34:41): There's this interesting question that everyone's asking right now. Mark Andreessen put it really well when he was on the pod. There's this kind of three-way standoff right now between PM's designers, engineers, where they each think they are the future and you don't need the other with AI. And everyone's wondering, what's the more important core skill? I imagine your sense is now AI makes designers even more powerful. And so this is even more the way to approach talk about just how you think this shifts this triad with AI enabling people.
turns.zh: 很兴奋能跟大家分享本季的支持赞助商Vanta。Vanta帮助超过15,000家公司（如Cursor、Ramp、Duolingo、Snowflake和Atlassian）赢得并证明客户的信任。得益于人工智能，团队构建和发布产品比以往任何时候都快。但随之而来的是产品和业务面临的风险空前增加。我接触过的每位安全负责人都深感保护组织、业务乃至客户数据的压力与日俱增。由于事态发展迅速，他们只能被动应对，不断猜测优先级，并被迫将就使用过时的解决方案。（00:34:14）：Vanta通过35项安全与隐私框架（包括SOC 2认证、ISO 27001和HIPAA）实现合规与风险管理自动化，助力企业快速达标并保持合规。信任比以往任何时候都更能决定企业的成败。欲了解更多信息，请访问vanta.com/lenny。作为本播客的听众，您可享受Vanta产品1000美元优惠，优惠链接为vanta.com/lenny。（00:34:41）：当前人们普遍面临一个有趣的困境。马克·安德森在播客中精辟地指出，当前产品经理、设计师和工程师之间存在三方博弈——他们各自认为自己是AI时代的未来主导者，无需依赖对方。人们不禁追问，哪种核心技能更重要？我认为AI让设计师的能力得到了极大提升，这无疑是探讨AI如何重塑三方博弈的绝佳视角。

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Well, it sounds highly dysfunctional if folks are having that standoff. That is not a good thing. But I do like that people are thinking about doing work really differently. I think that's imperative at this moment of time. The rate of change is extraordinary. Look, I do think designers feel vindicated in a lot of ways. A lot of designers had parents who were saying, "Why aren't you studying computer science? What are you going to do with this skillset drawing things? This doesn't make any sense." (00:35:37): And I think today, a lot of our designers are now shipping code, which is extraordinary. And that's a really big and really meaningful change in terms of the way that the design works here at Snap and the way the creative process works. And so I think removing friction from the creative process and being able to go from idea to impact at the scale of almost a billion people using Snapchat is really empowering and exciting for designers who feel like these tools maybe level the playing field to some extent for creative people.
turns.zh: 如果这种僵局持续下去，确实听起来很不正常。这可不是好事。不过我很欣赏人们正以全新的方式思考工作方式。在当下这个变革速度极快的时代，这种转变势在必行。看看，我确实觉得设计师们在很多方面都得到了认可。很多设计师的父母曾说：“你为什么不学计算机科学？学这门技能画画能有什么用？这根本说不通。”（00:35:37）：如今，我们许多设计师都能直接编写代码了，这实在令人惊叹。这对Snap的设计工作流程和创意流程都产生了重大且深远的影响。因此，我认为消除创意流程中的阻碍，让创意人员能以近十亿Snapchat用户的规模将创意转化为实际影响，这对设计师们来说既是赋能，也是令人兴奋的挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. What I feel like, I don't see this happening yet, but I feel like because now it's so much easier to build, people are shipping all these okay things and it feels like design should have its moment of glory right now as a differentiator of like, "Okay, this is actually awesome." I haven't felt that yet, and I'm curious if that's what will begin to happen.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得这种情况目前尚未出现，但我觉得由于现在构建产品变得容易得多，人们交付了很多还不错的成果，所以设计师现在应该迎来属于自己的辉煌时刻，成为差异化的存在。人们会说：“哇，这真的太棒了。”但我还没感受到这种情况，我很好奇这种情况是否会开始出现。

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Well, I think for us, design actually has always operated as a bottleneck at the company, which is incredibly important. It's intentional that things need to be approved by design to ship. And sometimes that really annoys people and it does slow down the shipping process. Sometimes it means that if you don't know how to work well with design or get your ideas in front of design, that some really innovative or cool new thing developed by a PM or developed by an engineer maybe doesn't get shipped as fast as it should. But that bottleneck is really, really important because that's what results in a cohesive customer experience. (00:37:01): And I think you can see when an app has been built by teams who are responsible for different pages of the app or different parts of the experience, but there isn't really a cohesive through line. And I think for us at Snap, having design really actually be that bottleneck in terms of helping to manage what we're shipping and what it looks like and how it all works together, I think is really important.
turns.zh:
嗯，我认为对我们来说，设计在公司里一直是一个至关重要的瓶颈环节。故意让设计部门审核后才能发布产品，这确实会让有些人感到烦躁，也会拖慢发布进度。有时候，如果你不懂得如何与设计团队合作，或者无法让你的创意得到他们的认可，那么产品经理或工程师开发的那些创新或酷炫新功能，可能就无法按预期快速上线。但这个瓶颈环节确实非常重要，因为它能确保为用户提供一致的体验。

（00:37:01）：你可以看到，有些应用是由负责不同页面或体验模块的团队开发的，但整体缺乏连贯性。在Snap，我们让设计团队成为这个瓶颈环节，负责把控发布内容的质量、外观设计以及整体协同效果，我认为这非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a good segue to something I wanted to ask you about, which is you're famously very in the weeds on everything that is going on, all the things that are shipping, you're very close to the pixels. I'm curious how that's evolved for you over time. Are you still in there looking at everything that's about to ship? And what's your just philosophy on founders having to be involved in, let's say, the pixels and the details of the product?
turns.zh: 接下来我想问你一个问题，你以往对所有正在进行的项目都了如指掌，特别是即将发布的功能，你总是深入到细节层面。我很好奇你这种工作方式是如何演变的。你现在还亲自审阅所有即将发布的功能吗？对于创始人来说，必须亲自参与产品的像素级细节和设计，你有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: First and foremost, yeah, this is what I love to do. I love building things. I love making new products, services for our community. That is what drives me. I really, really enjoy that part of the process. So it's not work to me. It's something that I really just love doing and love doing together with our team. And so I think for me, in addition to all the great people I get to work with here at Snap, the thing that wakes me up with a smile on my face every morning, the reason why I'm skipping to work is because I am in the weeds on what we're building and shipping to our community. That being said, there are always smarter, better, more talented experts working on all the different things that we have going on, but I really do like staying close to what we're creating. (00:38:32): I don't think it's relevant just to founders. I think no matter what type of company you're running or your role in the company, staying close to your customer, staying close to the product and the way that it's serving your customer is the fundamentally most important thing you could possibly do. I think I absolutely subscribe to the old school, walk the floors, talk to your customers, get out there and stay in touch with what's actually happening with your service, with your community, with your team. And I think that's probably the most important job that any leader can do in any company is stay close to their customers, stay close to their team.
turns.zh:
首先，没错，这正是我热爱做的事。我喜欢开发产品，喜欢为我们的社区创造新产品和新服务。这才是我的驱动力。我真的非常享受这个过程，所以对我来说，这根本不算工作，而是我热爱的事情，也是我和团队共同努力的方向。除了Snap这里优秀的团队，每天早上醒来面带微笑的原因，投入到我们为社区打造和发布的产品中，也是我每天迫不及待去工作的动力。话说回来，我们团队总有更聪明、更有才华的人负责不同的项目，但我确实喜欢紧跟我们正在创造的东西。

（00:38:32）：我认为这不仅适用于创始人，无论你经营什么类型的公司，或在公司中担任什么角色，与客户保持紧密联系、关注产品及其服务客户的方式，都是最重要的。我完全认同传统理念——走访各部门、与客户交流、深入了解服务实际情况、与团队保持沟通。对我来说，在任何公司里，与客户和团队保持紧密联系都是最重要的职责。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you feel like, especially for a consumer and consumer social product, this is extra important to just be extremely in the weeds on everything that is shipping and say having your design team have to approve everything. Do you feel like that's especially important for consumer?
turns.zh: 你觉得，特别是对于消费级和社交产品来说，深入了解所有即将发布的内容，尤其是让设计团队审核每个细节，这是否尤为重要？你认为这对面向消费者的产品来说尤其重要吗？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: I don't think it's especially important for consumer. I think it's especially important for any company that wants to deliver great products to their community. Companies have different points of strength and differentiation, but if you want to differentiate on the product experience, I think it's really important that leaders stay very close to that.
turns.zh: 我认为这对消费者来说并非特别重要。但对于任何希望为社区提供优质产品的公司而言，这都至关重要。不同公司各有专长和差异化优势，但若想在产品体验上脱颖而出，我认为领导层必须紧密贴近这一核心需求。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything special you look for in the designers you hire knowing that they're basically running the show and just approving everything and just kind of like the right hand to Evan? Is there anything in particular you look for when you're hiring these designers?
turns.zh: 既然你深知设计师们基本上是在掌控全局、只需批准设计方案，并充当埃文的得力助手，那你招聘设计师时会特别关注哪些方面呢？在招聘这些设计师时，是否有特定的要求？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Yeah, there's a couple really important things. First of all, we make all of our hiring decisions just based off portfolio. So that's really all we want to see. I really don't care where you've worked or your level of experience. In fact, most people join our design team right out of school, not from a big tech company or something like that. And really what I'm focused on is understanding the portfolio, and I want to see two things from the portfolio. The first is a really wide range, and that is the difference between art and design. So there are lots of people who have a very distinct style, right? They have a very distinct way of building things and creating things. That really is art, right? They're expressing themselves and their own personal point of view on the world, and it can be very beautiful, but it is not design. (00:40:35): Design is really about empathizing with your customer, empathizing with your audience, your viewer, whoever it is, and then building something that really resonates with them. And that means you need to have an extraordinary amount of range. You've got to be able to build and create things that look totally different. So when I'm going through a portfolio, the first thing I'm looking for is like, are they building stuff that all looks the same or are they building things that look really different that have been responsive to different sets of needs? And that's how I know that they're a designer and not just an artist. And then the other thing I want to understand, and typically I interview every designer that joins our team, and what I want to understand is why and the story behind the work that they created. (00:41:19): So typically what I'll do is just say, "Hey, pick something in your portfolio, anything you feel strongly about it." You could love it, hate it, I don't care. You just have to feel strongly about it. And just tell me the story of why you made it and what you learned through that process. And I think pretty quickly you can understand someone's process in terms of building something or inventing something, how do they go about it? And I'm really trying to make sure that we have people who have different ways of doing that on our team. One of the strengths of our design team has been that people come from lots of different backgrounds. They might come from 3D animation or they might come from electrical engineering. And that's a real strength to have folks who see the world differently and have totally different sets of skills.
turns.zh: 是的，有几个关键要点。首先，我们所有的招聘决策都仅基于作品集。这才是我们真正想看到的。我并不在意你曾在哪里工作或你的经验水平。事实上，我们设计团队的大多数成员都是刚从学校毕业的，并非来自大型科技公司之类的地方。我真正关注的是理解作品集，我希望从作品集中看到两点：第一，作品集要风格多样。这是艺术与设计的区别所在。很多人拥有非常独特的风格，对吧？他们构建和创作事物的方式截然不同。这确实是艺术，对吧？他们在表达自己和对世界的个人观点，这很美，但这不是设计。（00:40:35）设计真正在于与客户、受众、观众或任何相关方共情，然后打造真正能引起他们共鸣的东西。这意味着你需要拥有极其广泛的能力。你必须能够构建和创作风格迥异的作品。所以当我审阅作品集时，首先关注的是：他们的作品是千篇一律，还是因应不同需求而有所变化？这就是我判断他们是设计师而非艺术家的标准。接下来我想了解的，而且我通常会面试加入我们团队的每位设计师，那就是他们创作作品背后的初衷和故事。（00:41:19）所以我通常会让他们选出作品集中最引以为傲的作品，无论是喜爱还是厌恶，我都不在乎，只要他们对此有强烈感受即可。然后让我听他们讲述创作背后的故事和所获的启发。我认为很快就能理解一个人构建或发明某样东西的流程，他们是如何着手的？而我真正希望确保团队中拥有不同方法的人。我们的设计团队的优势之一就是成员背景多元，他们可能来自3D动画领域，也可能来自电气工程领域。能让不同视角看待世界、拥有完全不同技能组合的人共事，这确实是一大优势。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So as I was preparing for this chat, I talked to a bunch of people that worked at Snap over the years and I've integrated their ideas throughout already. But one that came up that I thought was interesting is I hear that you spent a lot of time developing young design talent and that's a big focus of yours. Can you just talk about how you develop young design talent?
turns.zh: 准备这次访谈时，我采访了多位曾在Snap工作过的人，并已将他们的见解融入其中。但其中有一点让我觉得很有意思——听说你们花了大量时间培养年轻设计人才，这也是你们的核心关注点。能否谈谈如何培养年轻设计人才？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Well, I think the number one way to develop young design talent is just help them make lots of stuff and get a lot of feedback from whether it's our customers or their teammates or myself directly. And so, one of the things that we do that's different at Snap is your first day that you join the design team, you present work. And it's really, really important that the first day that you show up on the team, you're making things. And that just sets the tone for the rest of your experience on the design team and growth on the design team because really that's what we're all about. And so I think folks who can get comfortable very quickly in that velocity of making things, that's where the ego sort of melts away because when you're creating a thousand new ideas, who cares that most of them are not great ideas? (00:43:02): That's totally fine. What we want to get rid of is that sense of preciousness that people have around ideas where they feel like, "Oh, I've got this one really perfect, great idea, and if people don't love it, that means that I'm not a great designer." It's like, no, that's ridiculous. We all need to just create as many ideas as possible that will lead us to some really great ideas hopefully over time. And so I think for young designers, establishing that velocity of ideation very early on is really, really important. And then the other thing we do that I think is different, although I don't know, I've never really worked anywhere else, is we don't allow designers to get stuck on specific products or verticals for very long. (00:43:44): We like to make sure people are rotating through different parts of the product to bring new ideas and fresh perspectives and also to avoid getting bored. If you're a great designer and you're stuck designing the chat experience for three years, I mean, how boring is that? It's really exciting, I think at Snap, to be able to work across all of these highly engaged product services. We have one of the largest maps in the world. We have the biggest augmented reality platform. These are really exciting opportunities for designers and it's important that we are rotating them across all of these different products so they're not getting stuck.
turns.zh: 我认为培养年轻设计人才的首要方法，就是帮助他们多创作作品，并从客户、团队成员或我本人那里获得大量反馈。在Snap，我们有个与众不同的做法：设计团队新人入职首日，便需展示作品。新人入职当天就能动手创作，这一点至关重要。这为他们在设计团队的整个经历奠定了基调，也推动了他们的成长，因为这正是我们的核心理念。那些能迅速适应这种高产创作节奏的人，其自负往往会被消解——毕竟当你构思上千个新创意时，谁会在意其中大部分都不算出色呢？（00:43:02）这完全没关系。我们要摒弃那种对创意的珍视心理，不必执着于“我有个完美绝伦的创意，若无人欣赏，就证明我不是优秀设计师”。这太荒谬了。我们需要尽可能多地产出创意，相信优秀的创意终将浮出水面。因此，我认为对年轻设计师而言，尽早建立这种高产的创意节奏至关重要。还有一点值得一提——虽然我从未在其他公司工作过，但Snap的做法确实与众不同：我们不允许设计师长期局限于特定产品或垂直领域。（00:43:44）我们会安排设计师轮换不同产品线，以引入新思路、新视角，同时避免倦怠感。如果你是个优秀设计师，却三年如一日专注于聊天体验开发，那得多无聊啊？在Snap，跨越多个高参与度产品服务的工作机遇令人兴奋不已。我们拥有全球规模最大的地图平台，最大的增强现实平台……这些对设计师而言都是绝佳的舞台，合理的轮岗安排能确保他们保持新鲜感。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I had Jenny Wen on the podcast. She was head of design for Claude and Cowork and she was like a director at Figma. And then she came to Anthropic and moved to just IC design again. And I asked her what's the hardest part of that move? And she said it's just all the crits that she has to deal with now are just so much criticism and constant feedback. And she forgot about that part of it. So it's interesting that's such a core part of the way you, like the thing that people have to learn essentially and get good at.
turns.zh: 我曾在播客中采访珍妮·文（Jenny Wen），她曾是Claude和Cowork的设计主管，也是Figma的总监，后来加入Anthropic，再次投身独立设计师工作。当时我问她转行最难的部分是什么？她说现在要面对的各种批评实在太多了，反馈铺天盖地。她完全忘记了这部分的重要性。这很有意思，因为这恰恰是你们的核心工作方式——也是人们必须学习并精通的关键技能。

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Well, and one of the things that's so important about our design team and our design culture, one of the things that we try to do is there is no gate to showing me work every week. So there is no ... Any idea, it doesn't matter how good people think it is, how bad it is, you can bring it to that design meeting, get it on the list and share your work and your idea. And that is so important because I think to your point, sometimes people over-rely on this critique process and great ideas get filtered out. And so I think creating this culture on the team where you can bring anything to the design meeting, there's no filtering process, I think is just so important.
turns.zh: 嗯，关于我们的设计团队和设计文化，有一点非常重要，那就是每周向我展示作品时没有任何门槛限制。所以无论大家觉得作品有多出色或多糟糕，都能带到设计会议上，将其列入日程并分享自己的想法。这点至关重要，因为正如你所说，有时人们过度依赖评审流程，导致优秀创意被埋没。因此，在团队中营造一种可以随时把作品带到设计会议、无需经过任何筛选的文化氛围，我认为这非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned AI, how designers are shipping code. I have a friend who works at a big tech company and you just said all the design team, they're required to ship like, I don't know, 10 PRs a month or something like that or a quarter, which is such a new world. I guess one is just like, how do you think about designers shipping code? Is that like just do it if you can or is there a requirement sort of thing? And broadly, I'm just curious how AI is changing the way your team operates. What are just a few things that have been impactful in how your team operates that are AI driven?
turns.zh: 你提到了人工智能，以及设计师们现在需要参与代码开发。我的一个朋友在一家大型科技公司工作，你刚才说整个设计团队每月要提交10个PR（代码合并请求），或者每个季度要完成多少个，这真是全新的工作模式。我很好奇，你如何看待设计师参与代码开发？是只要有能力就应该去做，还是有硬性要求呢？更广泛地说，我很想了解人工智能如何改变了团队的运作方式。哪些由人工智能驱动的创新举措对团队运作产生了显著影响？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Taking a step back, it's definitely not a requirement to ship code on the design team, but I think people are so passionate and curious about learning new things. I mean, one of the things we've always tried to do on the design team is just figure it out. I remember in the early days of some of the 3D graphic stuff that we were trying to do, one of our team members had never done 3D graphics before. And they're like, "Okay, let's just figure it out." So they took some online tutorials and boom, we were off to the races. So I think the design team has always been really flexible in terms of their curiosity, learning new things. And so I don't think you have to push people or create a requirement or something like that for folks to want to adopt new tools and want to ship code. (00:46:30): I think the big question now that everyone and anyone thinks they can submit a PR is like how we don't break things at a billion or nearly a billion user scale, right? That's really important. So I think what we've really tried to do is also develop AI tools and guardrails to make it easier for more people to participate and submit code, but also reduce the likelihood that we're going to have some sort of bug. So we've got automated code review now. We've, I think automatically detected like close to 10,000 bugs at this point probably. We have a system at Snap where on the internal version of the app, you can shake to report your problem and agents now debug exactly what happened, what went wrong and can actually suggest a fix. And I think in pretty short order it'll be implementing the fix as well, which is pretty crazy. (00:47:19): So I think taking a step back, there's so much excitement around the way that AI is going to change the way that companies work. Obviously software companies in particular, like ours, I think are on the cutting edge of the way that AI is changing how things get built and what gets done. We really wanted to bring some order to that chaos. And so the way that we did that was really by starting with the jobs to be done for our community and our advertisers. So getting really, really basic and straightforward on, okay, for Snap-chatters, our jobs to be done, it's as simple as like get people to download the app, get them to add their close friends, get them to, I don't know, use lenses, something like that. On the advertiser front, right? It could be bringing people into the ad platform, configuring their campaign, et cetera. (00:48:08): And so by listing out all these jobs to be done, really for the community journey and for advertisers as well, it became very clear where we could use agents, where we needed to be very focused in terms of building cross-functional teams around those jobs supported by AI tools. And it's also given us, I think, a really helpful mechanism to track our progress against the business outcomes for each of those jobs. So I think for us trying to, while I think in this moment of time, you certainly want to have a thousand flowers bloom and people are building agents and experimenting, I think at the same time, making sure that we stay focused on what matters to our community, what matters to advertisers is really, really important.
turns.zh:
退一步来说，设计团队并不一定要把代码上线，但我认为这里的人们对学习新事物充满热情和好奇心。我的意思是，我们设计团队一直努力做到的一件事就是想办法解决问题。记得在我们尝试做一些3D图形效果的早期阶段，有个团队成员从未接触过3D图形设计。他们就说："好吧，我们自己研究一下。"于是他们找了一些在线教程，很快就上手了。所以我觉得设计团队在好奇心和学习新事物方面一直非常灵活。因此，我认为没必要强制要求人们去采用新工具或上线代码。  

（00:46:30）：现在最大的问题是，每个人都觉得自己能提交PR（代码请求），但如何在十亿级甚至近十亿用户的规模下避免出问题呢？这非常重要。因此，我们致力于开发AI工具和安全机制，让更多人参与代码提交，同时降低出现漏洞的风险。比如我们现在有自动代码审查系统，估计已经检测出近1万个漏洞。Snap内部应用还有一个功能，用户遇到问题可以通过摇晃设备报告，智能客服会自动排查问题并给出修复建议，甚至直接帮用户实施修复，这真是太神奇了。  

（00:47:19）：退一步说，人们对AI将如何改变企业运作方式充满期待。显然，软件公司尤其是像我们这样的公司，正走在AI变革的尖端。我们希望为这种混乱带来秩序。我们的方法是从社区和广告主的核心需求出发。社区方面，用户只需下载应用、添加好友、使用滤镜等功能；广告主方面则包括引流至广告平台、配置活动等。  

（00:48:08）：通过列出这些核心任务，我们清晰地知道哪些任务可以用智能客服支持，哪些任务需要跨职能团队协作。这也为我们提供了追踪每个任务业务成果的有效机制。尽管当下我们鼓励百花齐放，支持大家探索智能客服，但同时确保聚焦于对社区和广告主真正重要的事情至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I want to take a step back and think about, just kind of reflect back. It's been 15 years since you've been working on Snap. You launched about 15 years ago. I'm curious just what are some of the maybe biggest lessons, maybe the hardest lessons you've learned over the past 15 years, things that you're like, "Oh, I didn't realize this as I was starting this company."
turns.zh: 好的。我想回顾一下过去，进行一下反思。Snap成立已经15年了。大约15年前我们正式上线。我很好奇，在过去的15年里，你学到的最重要的经验教训是什么，或者说最难的那些课程是什么？那些让你感叹“创业之初我根本没意识到这一点”的事情。

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Yeah, I think it's hard to comprehend how much the job changes over time. I mean, it's really quite extraordinary to go from my job in the early days with Bobby and I was helping design the product, but I was also answering customer support emails. I was trying to get our legal filing sorted out. I was trying to raise money. As the company grows and things evolve, so much more of the job is about leadership, about making sure you're really developing people, selecting the right people to be on the team, developing the culture, doing that really, really seriously. And in some ways, creating a structure that can enforce that to have a cohesive culture and a vision around the company, it becomes about strategy, managing through enormous change like what we're seeing with artificial intelligence today, but also several years ago, managing through the pandemic or managing through rebuilding our advertising platform as the landscape changed. (00:50:12): So the job has just changed so dramatically. And I think that's part of what's so energizing about it, what I enjoy so much about it, but it's also something I never in a million years could have anticipated when we were first getting started.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得很难理解这份工作会随时间发生多大的变化。我的意思是，从早期和鲍比一起工作，参与产品设计、回复客户支持邮件、处理法律文件、筹集资金，到公司发展壮大后更多地承担领导职责，确保团队成员成长、选拔合适人才、塑造企业文化，这些转变都令人惊叹。如今面对人工智能等颠覆性技术，我们需要制定战略应对变革；几年前应对疫情；重建广告平台以适应新环境……职位职责的变化实在太大了。这也是这份工作如此充满活力、让我乐在其中的原因，但在刚起步时，绝对是超出我想象的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How have you most changed and I guess evolved over that course? What's a big area that you've improved in?
turns.zh: 在这些变化中，你自身有哪些最显著的成长和进步？在哪些方面你有所提升？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: One of the big focus areas for me was learning how to communicate more effectively, both to our team, but also here on a podcast or with the world, I mean, so much of the job is about becoming a great communicator. I remember I had the opportunity to meet President Clinton at one point in the early days of the company and he was like, "It's very interesting, being president is really being explainer in chief and your job is actually to just explain stuff to people and help them make sense of the world and the company and their role in it." And I always thought that was really interesting. And I go back to that a lot. (00:51:06): So much of my job is to explain things to our company and to our shareholders, to the world in ways that really make sense and can inspire folks and help us to all move in the right direction. So I think communication just becomes such a core skill. And I think in the early days, I was unnecessarily dismissive of the really important role of communication.
turns.zh: 对我来说，一个关键的提升方向就是学习如何更有效地沟通——无论是与团队成员交流，还是在播客中与外界对话。毕竟，领导力很大程度上在于成为一名优秀的沟通者。我记得公司早期有机会见克林顿总统，他曾说：“总统的角色就是要充当首席解释官，你的职责就是向人们解释世界、公司以及他们在其中的角色。”这句话让我深有共鸣。如今我也经常回想这句话。（00:51:06）我的大部分工作就是用易于理解的方式向公司、股东和外界传达信息，激发人们的共鸣，推动我们朝着正确的方向前进。所以我认为沟通能力已然成为核心技能。而在早期，我对沟通的重要性却不以为然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For founders that are hearing this and they're like, "Okay, I'm going to work on this," What most helped you level up in this space? Is it like coaches? Is it people around you? Is it just doing it?
turns.zh: 对于听众中的创业者来说，他们可能会想：“好吧，我要在这方面下功夫。”那么，哪些因素最能帮助你提升这方面的能力？是导师的指导？身边人的支持？还是纯粹的实践？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Just doing it is really the only way. And I remember that was really the advice one of our board members gave to me because I was so reluctant. I didn't want to do an all hands. I didn't want to do Q&A. In the early days of the company, I was like, "I'll just send an email." And he's like, "What are you doing?" He's like, "Too bad, Evan. This is your job." And I think that was really, really good advice. And so literally I was like, "Okay, fine. This is a core part of my job and what I need to learn how to do. I'm going to learn to love it. I want to love it. I want to get up there and get in front of our company and really enjoy answering all these really tough questions and digging into the business with our team." And now I really do. (00:52:19): I've learned to really enjoy that dialogue with our team. And I learned so much from the questions that folks ask. And I love that openness. I think it's just such an important part of our company and who we are.
turns.zh: 光是去做就是唯一的办法。我记得我们一位董事会成员曾对我这么说——因为我当时特别不情愿。我不想开全体会议，不想做问答环节。在公司早期，我总想：“我只需发封邮件就行了。” 他却说：“你在干什么？” 他说：“太遗憾了，埃文。这是你的职责。” 我觉得这真是个非常明智的建议。于是我决定：“好吧，这是我的核心职责，我必须学会如何做好。我要学会享受这个过程。我想喜欢上它。我要站在公司台前，认真回答那些尖锐的问题，与团队一起深入探讨业务。” 现在我确实做到了。（00:52:19）我学会了享受与团队的这种对话，也从大家的问题中收获了许多。我喜欢这种开放的氛围。我认为这对我们公司和我们的文化至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I had Rahul Vohra on the podcast a while back, the founder of Superhuman. I don't know if this is what you went through, but he went through a transition where he loved what he was doing and then ended up being pushed by VCs and leaders to like, okay, you got to do these other things. And then like, okay, I really don't like this and I'm going to find a way to do the thing I really enjoy because that's going to reflect in so many ways across the business and help us succeed." Is that something you went through, where just like, okay, I just want to get back to the product and building?
turns.zh: 不久前，我在播客上采访了Superhuman的创始人拉胡尔·沃拉。我不知道你是否有过类似经历，但他也经历过转变——起初热爱自己的工作，后来被风投和高管们催促去做其他事情。最终他说：“好吧，我不喜欢这些事，我要找到自己真正热爱的工作。”因为这会对整个公司产生深远影响，助力我们取得成功。

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: I think that's only partly true if you want to stay in the CEO job. I think the CEO job has a lot of requirements that are not necessarily things that you love to do in the morning. There's a huge amount of responsibility that comes along with being CEO. There's a lot of operational rigor that I think needs to be developed. I think not every part of the CEO job is glamorous. So I think if I just wanted to work on product, I would pick a different job at Snap. But I think because I really like leading our company and leading the direction and strategy for the business, and because I see a huge opportunity in transforming the way that people use computing in the future, both through Snapchat, but also with specs, I think this is the right role for me right now. I mean, certainly I would spend more time with my family and probably have more fun on some days if I was in a different role or more focused on design. (00:53:57): But I think the opportunity for a business like ours at the scale that we have, it's a once in a lifetime opportunity for me. And despite its challenges, I do like the CEO job.
turns.zh: 我认为如果你想继续担任CEO一职，这话只对了一半。CEO职位有很多职责，这些未必是你早上最爱做的事。CEO肩负着巨大的责任，需要培养运营的严谨性。我认为CEO工作并非全是光鲜亮丽的。所以如果我只想专注产品，我本可以选择Snap的其他职位。但我真的很喜欢领导公司，引领业务方向和战略，而且我看到了未来通过Snapchat和Specs改变人们使用计算方式的巨大机遇。我觉得这份工作目前很适合我。当然，如果换个角色或更专注于设计，我能有更多时间陪家人，也能享受更多乐趣。（00:53:57）但我认为像我们这样的公司，拥有这样的规模，这对我来说是千载难逢的机会。尽管面临挑战，我还是喜欢CEO这份工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So kind of along those lines, you put out this letter, I think it was the end of last year where you described this coming year as the crucible moment for Snap. It's so interesting just like you guys have a billion monthly active users. That's just absurd. I don't think people realize this. You're making six billion a year in revenue, something like that. One of the very few social networks that lasts that is durable with a very valuable, interesting audience. On the flip side, the stock hasn't been killing it. There's like these investors coming at you trying to tell you to change all these things. I guess just thoughts, reflections, and what do you think people are missing about where this might go?
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，你去年年底发布了一封信，称未来一年是Snap的关键时刻。真有意思，你们有10亿月活用户，这太惊人了。我觉得人们对此没有充分认识。你们每年营收60亿美元左右，是少数能持续且拥有高价值、引人入胜用户群体的社交网络之一。另一方面，股价表现不佳。投资者不断施压，要求你们做出改变。我想就此谈谈你的看法、反思，以及你认为人们忽视了哪些关键点？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Well, that's really one of the reasons why I called this year a crucible moment. I mean, the company's almost at the scale of entering the Fortune 500, which is really exciting. It's almost at a billion monthly active users. It's about to launch specs after 12 years of investment in this future computing platform, but at the same time, it's still not net income profitable, for example, because we've been investing so heavily in the future and making the choice to do that. And so I think this is the year that we have to prove that Snapchat can be a really strong, profitable business, that it continues to grow both in terms of the reach of our audience and their engagement with new products, whether it's topic chats or spotlight, or I think we've got 200 million people playing games every month on Snapchat now. So gaming is becoming a big part of the engagement drivers on Snapchat. (00:55:50): And the reason why that's so important is that it's going to be very hard for us to win long-term in specs without a really solid foundation. And so I think we need to demonstrate that after a couple years of rebuilding our ad platform, rebuilding our go to-market efforts, really accelerating the growth of the small medium customer part of our business, which has grown really rapidly for us that this year we have a really solid foundation to launch the next chapter in the company's history. So it's a real turning point for Snap that's really exciting, but it's definitely an all hands on deck moment for the company.
turns.zh: 嗯，这确实是我把今年称为关键时刻的原因之一。我是说，公司的规模已经接近进入《财富》500强，这真的很令人兴奋。我们的月活跃用户即将突破10亿大关。经过12年的投资后，我们即将推出Specs平台，但与此同时，公司尚未实现净利润盈利，例如，因为我们一直在大力投资未来，并做出了这样的选择。所以我认为今年我们必须证明Snapchat可以成为一个强大且盈利的业务，无论是在用户覆盖范围还是新产品互动方面——无论是话题聊天、Spotlight，还是我认为现在Snapchat上每月有2亿人玩游戏。游戏正成为Snapchat用户参与度的重要驱动力。（00:55:50）：而这一点之所以如此重要，是因为如果没有一个坚实的基础，我们就很难在Specs上赢得长期胜利。因此，我认为在重建广告平台、重建市场推广策略、真正加速中小客户业务增长（这一业务对我们来说增长非常迅速）几年后，今年我们将为公司历史的新篇章奠定坚实基础。所以这对Snap来说是一个真正的转折点，确实令人兴奋，但对公司来说无疑也是一个全力以赴的时刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You had a really interesting way of describing Snap in the market. You called Snap the middle child. Talk about just what that means.
turns.zh: 你用一种非常有趣的方式描述了Snap在市场中的地位。你称Snap是中间孩子。能谈谈这意味着什么吗？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Yeah. I think one of the things that's so funny about our service is that while we're very, very large in terms of the scale of our audience, in terms of the scale of our business, we're much larger than a Pinterest or Reddit, for example, we're also way smaller than Meta and Google. And so we occupy this very interesting sort of middle position in the market. And I think that comes with a lot of benefits because we're big enough. We have enough scale to do really interesting things, but it also comes with the challenges of being overshadowed in some cases by our older brothers and maybe sometimes the younger kids are getting more attention. And so I think again, as in this crucible moment, it's part of defining who we are as a company and who we are as a business. (00:57:13): And I think one of the things that will play an important role in that is getting specs out to consumers because I think right now we've talked so long about the role that specs will play in the world. We've worked on developing the platform for so long, but without something that you can really play with and hang onto and use yourself, it's hard to really understand the next chapter of Snap's journey. So I think one of the biggest challenges that middle children face is defining themselves, standing out from their older siblings and younger siblings. And so I think this is a moment and a year when Snap is really going to define itself, and I'm really excited about that.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为我们服务的一个非常有趣的地方是，虽然我们在观众规模和业务规模方面非常大——比如比Pinterest或Reddit大得多——但我们也远小于Meta和谷歌。因此，我们在市场上占据了一个非常有趣的中间位置。我认为这带来了很多好处，因为我们足够大，有足够的规模去做一些有趣的事情，但也带来了被大哥们盖过风头、甚至有时被小弟们获得更多关注的挑战。所以我认为，就像在这一关键时刻一样，这是定义我们作为公司和业务身份的一部分。（00:57:13）：我认为在这方面起重要作用的一件事是向消费者推出Specs，因为我认为我们现在已经谈论了很久Specs将在世界上发挥的作用。我们已经为开发这个平台工作了很久，但如果没有你可以真正玩耍、留存和使用的东西，就很难真正理解Snap下一章的旅程。所以我认为中间孩子面临的最大挑战之一就是定义自己，从哥哥和弟弟中脱颖而出。所以我认为这是一个时刻和一年，在这一年里，Snap将真正定义自己，我对此非常兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of middle child, you have a number of children and I'm curious, there's a whole going in a whole different direction. What's your just policy on screens and devices? Having built Snapchat and then also specs, just how do you think about devices and your kids?
turns.zh: 说到中间孩子，你有几个孩子，我很好奇，你对屏幕和设备的政策是什么？在创建了Snapchat和Specs之后，你如何看待设备和你的孩子？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Well, we've got a real range. We've got four boys, two, six, seven, and 15. So we approach it very differently for all the kids at different ages. For the two-year-old, it's like zero screen time. We really just want to essentially read with him and play, explore outside and those sorts of things, but not really focus on screens unless he is getting a haircut because he really struggles with getting his haircut. So when he gets a haircut, he really loves Bobcat tractors, those four-wheel sort of Bobcat tractors, and he loves to watch YouTube videos of people driving Bobcat tractors around. So when he gets his haircut, he can watch people drive Bobcat tractors. (00:58:54): But other than that, no screen time. For the six and seven-year-olds, they are, I would say, infrequent movie watchers. But other than that, again, we don't give them phones or anything like that. In fact, it was really fun over the holidays for Christmas, I gave them that new ... I think Palmer Lucky has a startup where they are sort of remaking Gameboys.
turns.zh: 嗯，我们的做法因年龄而异。家里有四个孩子，分别是两岁、六岁、七岁和十五岁。所以针对不同年龄段的孩子，我们采取了截然不同的方法。对于两岁的孩子，基本上没有屏幕时间。我们主要陪他阅读、玩耍、户外探索之类的，除非他去理发时需要看视频，因为他特别抗拒理发。每次理发后，他就痴迷于看YouTube上别人驾驶Bobcat拖拉机的视频。（00:58:54）不过除此之外，他基本不看屏幕。六岁和七岁的孩子，我觉得他们偶尔会看电影，但除此之外，我们也不给他们手机之类的东西。事实上，圣诞节假期的时候，我给他们买了新玩意儿……我记得Palmer Lucky公司正在重新制作Gameboy游戏机。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I have one of those.
turns.zh: 是啊，我也有一个。

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Yeah, it's really fun. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，很有趣。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mod retro.
turns.zh: 复古风。

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Yeah, mod retro. So the TBPN guys gave me two of them for our kids for Christmas. And so they get to spend a little time on those in addition to watching movies every now and then. And then with the 15-year-old, he is all in on technology, whether he's using it for school or whether he's using it to talk with his friends or using Snapchat. So it really depends on kids and where they're at developmentally, but I think for us, that's been our approach.
turns.zh: 对，复古风。所以TBPN团队的同事圣诞节送了我们两个这样的设备给孩子们。除了偶尔看电影，他们还能玩一玩。至于十五岁的孩子，他完全沉浸在科技世界里，无论是学习还是和朋友聊天、用Snapchat。总之，这取决于孩子的年龄和发展阶段，但我觉得我们家一直秉持这样的教育理念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything you're doing with AI in your kids, maybe even the older one, just AI education sort of tools, ChatGPT?
turns.zh: 你们有没有在AI教育方面做过尝试，比如给大孩子用ChatGPT之类的工具？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Yeah, it's so funny. At the breakfast table the other morning, actually, I was just asking them a lot about how are their teachers talking about AI at school? How are they thinking about integrating in the curricula Are you guys using AI all the time? And I think the answer so far has been not really, which I think is interesting, but certainly our kids play around with it at home. Our beta testers for specs, which is really fun. I really love using the glasses together with them and some of the really cool experiences there. And Flynn, who's the eldest is probably most fluent in using AI tools. But what I think is so fun, as a kid, I think all of us as kids are incredibly imaginative. We're all born creative. We have all these amazing ideas to share. And I think what's so cool about AI is how in nearly an instant, you can take any idea you have and make something. (01:00:40): And so I think that's so empowering for young people. It's certainly an experience I want our kids to have. And I think it's going to be so important to deeply integrate into the way that education works today.
turns.zh: 是啊，很有意思。前几天早餐桌上，我一直在问他们老师在学校怎么讲AI？课程里怎么整合AI？他们用得多吗？目前答案是用得不多，我觉得挺有意思的。不过孩子们在家倒是经常玩。我们是AI的测试用户，真的很有趣。我喜欢和他们一起用眼镜，体验那些超酷的功能。大儿子Flynn用AI工具最熟练了。我觉得孩子们天生就充满想象力，是天生的创造者，总有超多奇思妙想。AI最酷的地方在于，你几乎能瞬间把任何想法变为现实。这对年轻人来说太有力量了。我希望孩子们能接触到AI，相信这对教育未来至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It's interesting. Snapchat has always been really good at allowing you to create and feel like a superstar, just create all these really crazy lenses and filters and all these things. And it's interesting AI, just like vibe coding just unleashes so much creativity. And kids are so imaginative already.
turns.zh: 是啊。有意思的是，Snapchat一直很擅长激发创造力，比如让用户制作各种滤镜和特效。AI技术，比如Vibe Coding，能释放无限创造力。孩子们本来就天生富有想象力。

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So interesting. Okay. Well, to close out our conversation, I've got a couple. I'm going to take us to a couple corners, recurring corners on the podcast. One is AI corner. So the question is, what's a way you use AI in your, let's say, work that is just interesting that might be interesting for other people to learn from?
turns.zh: 太有趣了。好的。最后，想和大家分享几个话题，这些都是播客中经常讨论的领域。第一个是人工智能专题。我的问题是，在你们的工作中，有什么有趣的方式运用人工智能，或许其他人也能从中借鉴？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Well, one of the things that I really love about AI, at Snap, I've got access to all of our dashboards and documents and data. And so we have Glean that integrates all this data for me. And I've built just an agent that will go and comb through everything that's happening in the company and let me know what's up, what I need to focus on, what I need to catch. And every now and then it really catches something that I hadn't realized or need to focus a bit more on. And so I think we're just so fortunate to have so much structured data in our company. I mean, for our leaders, they also send me every week the three things from the week and three things looking ahead. (01:02:01): And so I can very, very easily get a sense for the hotspots in the company, the priority areas, and combined with all of our dashboards and metrics about the way that people are using our service. I feel like I have a really good sense for what's happening in the company. So I think what's been most exciting for me in terms of AI is that it's enabling, I think, the type of leadership structure that I've always wanted, which is very flat, very fast moving. And I think having an AI copilot to help me do that's been a big deal.
turns.zh: 嗯，在Snap，我最喜欢人工智能的一点是，我可以访问公司的所有仪表板、文档和数据。Glean会把所有这些数据整合起来，然后我开发了一个智能助手，它能自动筛选公司内发生的一切事情，提醒我需要关注的重点。每隔一段时间，它总能发现一些我之前没注意到或者需要深入研究的信息。公司有如此丰富的结构化数据真是太幸运了。比如，领导层每周都会给我发送本周三件要事和未来三个月的计划。（01:02:01）这样我就能非常清晰地掌握公司的热点领域和优先事项，再结合所有仪表板和用户使用服务的数据指标，我就能准确把握公司的动态。所以对我来说，人工智能最令人兴奋的地方在于，它为我实现了理想的领导架构——扁平化、高效运作。有了人工智能助手的支持，这真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that agent was, you built it in Glean. Is that where it lives?
turns.zh: 那个智能助手是在Glean里开发的吗？它存储在那里吗？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, that I've done in Glean, which is great. Obviously you can build all sorts of stuff in Cloud, but Glean for us is the most secure way to access all of our different documents and dashboards and things like that.
turns.zh: 是的。我是在Glean里开发的，这个平台很棒。当然，你可以在云端开发各种应用，但对我们来说，Glean是访问所有文档和仪表板最安全的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything interesting in your AI stack? There's sounds like Lean, Cloud. Is there anything else that's interesting maybe some people may not think about?
turns.zh: 你们的人工智能栈里还有其他有趣的部分吗？比如Lean、Cloud之类的。还有什么可能不为人知的亮点吗？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: I think one of the things that we're thinking a lot about is just taking the entire workflow and enabling it with an agent. So for example, taking a product idea and with our go to-market agent, taking that product idea, writing the spec, identifying the relevant folks who need to be involved in sign-offs and understanding it, actually helping to do the risk analysis on the product from a legal, trust and safety perspective, writing the go to-market materials like the blog, et cetera. We're working now on actually building the visuals as well, but doing that in one shot is really wild. (01:03:32): So I think there's all sorts of examples like that across the company in terms of the way that agents can play a really massive role in changing the way that we work. And that's connected to how we think about those jobs to be done. So if we can define a job to be done clearly enough that we can build an agent to do it, that can really create a lot of lift.
turns.zh: 我们现在重点考虑的是将整个工作流程通过智能助手实现自动化。比如，接到一个产品创意后，我们会用市场推广助手来撰写产品说明，识别需要参与签字的人员，进行风险分析，从法律、信任和安全角度把关产品，还能制作市场推广材料如博客等。我们现在还在开发可视化内容，但一次性完成所有这些工作真是太棒了。（01:03:32）所以我认为整个公司里有很多类似的例子，说明智能助手如何能极大地改变我们的工作方式。这也与我们对“待办事项”的定义息息相关。只要能清晰地定义一个任务，让智能助手去执行，就能带来巨大的效率提升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where do you build this agent? What's the platform to use?
turns.zh: 这个智能助手是在哪里开发的？用的是哪个平台？

turns.speaker: Evan Spiegel
turns.en: We've been using Claude to do a lot of the work across Snap. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我们在Snap内部一直用Claude来处理很多工作。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
